newsitem.title: CANADA: APEC ministers to discuss air liberalization.
newsitem.headline: APEC ministers to discuss air liberalization.

text.p: Transportation ministers from Asia-Pacific countries will meet in Canada this week to discuss liberalisation of air travel and ways to speed trade flows.
The two-day meeting in Victoria, British Columbia will gather ministers from the 18 members of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

On Monday, the officials and industry leaders will hold a forum with sessions on the outlook for air travel, urban transit, road, rail and ship transport, and ways to make links between different transportation modes more efficient.
The ministers will then meet on their own Tuesday and discuss priorities for further work in the run-up to a summit of APEC leaders in Vancouver in November.
One of APEC's main drives is to free trade among member economies and efficient transportation links are seen as an important way to underpin that effort, officials said.
"There is a need to overcome some severe congestion if the region is going to see sustained trade growth," said Paul Irwin of the Asia Pacific Foundation in Vancouver.

One of the more controversial topics for discussion at the meeting is air liberalisation, officials said. A working group has drafted eight recommendations toward freeing up air travel that will be discussed at the meeting.
"Some economies are quite keen and would like to move forward ... but some are opposed," said Kevin Kavanaugh, an official in Canada's transportation ministry.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater and Japan's Transport Minister Makoto Koga will hold separate bilateral talks during the APEC meeting to discuss longstanding differences on aviation.
Proponents of greater airline liberalisation point to the benefits of so-called "open-skies" agreements like the one between the United States and Canada that eliminate air travel barriers.
But some countries, especially small nations who do not have major regional airlines, are reluctant to have bigger foreign carriers gain equal access to their market.

The ministers will consider a proposal to expand bilateral air agreements between some countries to include cargo as well as passenger transport. Another suggestion would free carriers to set up their own ground support operations in foreign airports, something that is barred by some countries.
Some countries also want to allow airlines flying from one country to another to pick up passengers in a third country, a practice not permitted by some countries currently.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
